learner_notice: Commit one response before feedback appears. Entry checks are low stakes; an unresolved fresh re-entry returns control without exit credit.

items.title: Starting check: narrower serial tube
items.prompt: A steady incompressible fluid enters a narrower section of one unbranched tube. No leak occurs. What happens to average speed?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Guided practice: calculate serial speed
items.prompt: A tube area decreases from 6 cm² to 2 cm². If the initial speed is 3 m/s, what is the new speed for steady incompressible flow?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Less help: use radius squared
items.prompt: The radius of a serial tube decreases by a factor of two. What happens to speed if volume flow rate stays constant?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: On your own: equal branch split
items.prompt: A parent tube carries 15 mL/s and divides equally into five identical branches. What is the flow rate in each branch?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Near exit: serial area ratio
items.prompt: Section B has three times the area of Section A in one steady incompressible tube. How does vB compare with vA?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Changed exit: unequal branch areas
items.prompt: A 20 mL/s parent flow divides equally by flow rate into two branches. Branch X has twice the area of Branch Y. How do their speeds compare?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: continuity order
items.prompt: Which sequence correctly solves a serial continuity problem?
options: Set radii times speeds equal without squaring.
Set pressures equal before reading areas.
Add the two speeds and divide by area.
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: diameter change
items.prompt: A tube diameter triples while Q stays constant. What happens to average speed?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: junction ledger
items.prompt: Which equation represents a steady no-leak parent splitting into three branches?
options: Qparent + Q1 + Q2 + Q3 = 0 with all values positive
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: mixed branch sizes
items.prompt: A 24 mL/s parent splits into branches carrying 8 and 16 mL/s. Both branches have the same area. How do their speeds compare?
options: The 8 mL/s branch is twice as fast.
The 16 mL/s branch is twice as fast.
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Starting check: equal-height tradeoff
items.prompt: Along one ideal streamline at equal height, speed is greater at Point B than Point A. How does static pressure compare?
options: No relation is possible under the stated model.
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Guided practice: calculate pressure change
items.prompt: Horizontal water flow speeds up from 2 m/s to 6 m/s. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³. What is P2 − P1 under the ideal model?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Less help: height increase
items.prompt: An ideal fluid has the same speed at a point 2 m higher on the same streamline. What happens to static pressure?
options: It stays equal at every height.
It becomes zero in all fluids.
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: On your own: identify the valid model
items.prompt: Which condition is required for the simple Bernoulli relation used in this lesson?
options: Strong viscous loss with no correction
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Near exit: pressure at a constriction
items.prompt: A horizontal ideal tube narrows. Continuity shows speed doubles in the narrow section. What happens to static pressure there?
options: It is set only by tube color.
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Changed exit: compare speed and height
items.prompt: Point B is higher than A on an ideal streamline and has the same static pressure. What must be true about speed if no energy is added?
options: Speed is unrelated to height under Bernoulli.
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: write all three terms
items.prompt: Which expression is the ideal Bernoulli ledger used here?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: horizontal speed change
items.prompt: Along a horizontal ideal streamline, speed falls from 5 m/s to 3 m/s. What happens to static pressure?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: trace the height–speed tradeoff
items.prompt: Two points on an ideal streamline have equal static pressure, and the downstream point is higher. No pump or loss is present. Which term tradeoff determines the speed change?
options: Both height and kinetic terms rise while total energy stays fixed.
Pressure rises enough to pay for height despite pressures being equal.
Height has no role once the fluid is moving.
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: compare raised-section speed
items.prompt: Water flows from a lower garden-pipe section to a raised section on the same ideal streamline. Static pressure is equal at both sections, and no device adds energy. How does speed at the raised section compare?
options: It is greater because height and speed always rise together.
It is lower at the raised section.
It is equal because equal pressure forces equal speed at any height.
It cannot be compared even with Bernoulli assumptions.
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Starting check: Venturi throat
items.prompt: In a horizontal ideal Venturi tube, how do speed and static pressure at the narrow throat compare with upstream?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Guided practice: pitot speed
items.prompt: A pitot measurement in a fluid of density 800 kg/m³ gives Pstagnation − Pstatic = 1600 Pa. What is the ideal speed?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Less help: identify stagnation pressure
items.prompt: A forward-facing pitot opening brings a small sampled streamline locally to rest. Which pressure is measured there?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: On your own: compare pitot differences
items.prompt: Two measurements use the same fluid. Device A has twice the stagnation-minus-static pressure difference of Device B. How do ideal speeds compare?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Near exit: distinguish devices
items.prompt: A diagram compares pressure at a wide flowing section with pressure at a narrow flowing throat. Which device principle is being used?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Changed exit: infer from pressure ports
items.prompt: A probe records static pressure through a side port and a larger pressure through a forward-facing port at the same location. What does their difference represent ideally?
options: A Venturi area ratio by itself
Viscous loss with no speed information
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: identify the pressure pair
items.prompt: Which observation identifies a pitot rather than Venturi measurement?
options: Both ports sample moving sections of different area.
A tube narrows and throat static pressure falls.
Only the branch flow rates are summed.
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: throat comparison
items.prompt: A horizontal tube narrows while two side ports measure static pressure upstream and at the throat. Which pressure is lower ideally?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: pitot equation order
items.prompt: Which equation correctly infers ideal speed from a pitot pressure pair?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: density effect
items.prompt: Two fluids produce the same pitot pressure difference, but Fluid X has four times the density of Fluid Y. How do ideal speeds compare?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.
